E. D.

E. D.

This book by T.H. Paul presents a clearly structured and well articulated form of psychotherapy which integrates two major therapeutic approaches—the client centered counseling of Carl Rogers and psychoanalysis. By combining the non-directive mode of Rogers and the interpretive mode of psychoanalysis Paul comes up with a unique form of therapy which in some respects resembles modern psychoanalysis. Although Paul identifies his method as interpretive, many of his non-directive interpretations would be recognized by modern analysts as forms of joining and supporting the patient's resistance.

The book was written primarily as a textbook for students of psychotherapy and its major value lies in the wealth of illustrations of therapist/patient interchanges presented for the student's consideration. The book is organized as a series of paradigms consisting of simulated transcripts of therapy sessions. Paul analyzes each of these paradigms and discusses the technical and conceptual principles involved in formulating specific clinical interventions which illustrate the application of his technique. Among the paradigms presented are: “The Basic Instruction Paradigm,” “The Interpretive Paradigm,” and the “Resistance Paradigm.

Wekstein emphasizes that suicide prevention, identification, and treatment is multidisciplinary. He has prepared an overview where, perhaps, a multiauthored text covering historical, statistical, psychoanalytical, and sociological aspects is really needed.

An informative section of the handbook concerns the extremely high rate of psychopathology among medical students, physicians, and psychiatrists. These three groups (which include women) have at least double the general population suicide rate. The statistics reinforce the reviewer's opinion that individual and group psychotherapy should be a condition for admission to medical school and a condition for graduation.

Wekstein also clarifies normal suicidal attitudes in contrast to morbid attitudes. He suggests that acute psychosis may be a suicide preventive, whereas, in the recovery phase, failure to cope may signify a danger period. Although schizophrenics do not have a higher suicide rate than others, the psychoneurotic is at risk.

In this book Paul Watzlawick, who is a world authority on human communication and communication therapy, examines the basie elements of therapeutic communication. He points out that the usual procedure of interpreting the patient's communications into the rational and intellectual language of a particular therapeutic school of thought, contradicts the way in which the mind operates. Although a patient's communications in therapy are understood by the analyst to arise from unconscious, “dark” areas of his mind, analysts persist in trying to translate these communications, through interpretations, into the language of reason and consciousness. Watzlawick uses current evidence from brain research that identifies the differing function of right and left brain hemispheres, to refute the widely held belief that interpretation is the most effective form of therapeutic communication.

Jane Unger  

Psychoanalysis and National Health Insurance

The issues implicit in the implementation of national health insurance are of vital concern to mental health practitioners. The United States is the only industrial nation that has not yet instituted a comprehensive health insurance program, and it seems certain that a plan will eventually be adopted. Questions such as what benefits will be provided, whose service will be reimbursed, and how the program will be funded, need answers.

If mental health coverage is provided, the disciplines of psychology, social work, and psychoanalysis either will be part of the health care system or they will be excluded, and medical practitioners will provide the sole insurable services. Segments of organized psychiatry propose the “remedicalization” of psychotherapy so that only the organic brain syndromes and the psychoses would be defined as insurable illnesses.

In a 1977 report to the Kaiser-Permamente Medical Center, R. Harrington suggests that persons suffering from emotional distress, including psychoneuroses and character disorders, be referred to community colleges for courses in the art of living. The American Psychiatric Association has also been at work politically on a revision of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Diseases (DSM III). Although the attempt is being made to devise medically-based categories treatable only by physicians, in a recent test case in Wisconsin, a bill introduced implying that only physicians could practice “medical psychotherapy,” was not enacted.

Feelings: Our Vital Signs. By Willard Gaylin. New York: Harper and Row, 1979. 254 pp.

Richard Friedman

Richard Friedman

Richard Friedman  

In Feelings, Willard Gaylin has written a book which has both popular appeal as well as something to say to practicing psychoanalysts. He achieves this feat in two ways: through his beautiful simple style in which he makes sophisticated and subtle ideas clear and understandable and by establishing himself as such a decent person that one is charitably disposed to see the wisdom in his observations. What is not always clear, however, is his purpose for writing the book. Although Gaylin is a psychoanalyst, the book does not seem to have been written for psychoanalysts. He confuses psychoanalysis and psychiatry, something that is presumably irksome to most people in both professions, although perhaps this one lapse in his gentility stems from his own membership in both professions. There is a striking absence of case material; all examples are either literary or autobiographical.

His primary concern is with feelings which he says can only be understood anecdotally. Gaylin is more than just a good story teller. He finds feelings in an astonishingly wide range of literature and is as comfortable quoting his daughter as he is Virginia Woolf or Herodotus. But the purpose of the book does not seem to be to suggest new applications of psychoanalysis to literature or to familial reminiscences, however well he demonstrates the technique. Rather, although he does not say this himself, he seems to have written this book to develop the idea that all feelings are important and that every individual should, if possible, accept his or her feelings without acting on them. Gaylin juxtaposes the primacy of feelings to the more conventional psychoanalytic emphasis on insight, thoughts and ideas which he says have ‘ironically’ dominated psychoanalytic thinking.

Gaylin interprets Freud as a philosophical idealist and a spokesman for a kind of subjectivity bordering on solipsism: “No one, he [Freud] announced, lives in the real world. We occupy a space of our own creation—a collage compounded of bits and pieces of actuality arranged into a design determined by our internal perceptions, our hopes, our fears, our memories and our anticipation.

E. D.

Nathan Lietes has written a book that challenges the cardinal contention of psychoanalysis, that only transference interpretations are effective. He examines the status of this contention at length and makes explicit a variety of reasons for affirming or denying it.

Although Leites does not question that transference and transference interpretations are “central” to psychoanalysis, he does question that “all is transference”. Leites uses an abundance of case material to examine the following questions: Are reactions toward the analysis reactions toward the analyst? Do reactions toward the analyst dominate the hour? Do reactions toward the analyst dominate the patient's life?

He concludes that while the answer to the above is no doubt yes “for many patients at many moments of their analysis,” there is also a high incidence of non transference reactions that take place in analysis. As a result of his study, Leites suggests that the belief in the sole effectiveness of transference interpretation be abondoned.

Few concepts within psychoanalytic theory have grown in importance so dramatically as has that of countertransference. Lawrence Epstein and Arthur Feiner have compiled an eminently readable collection of articles covering the breadth of current thinking and presenting an overview of the shifting role of countertransference in the history of psychoanalytic theory from Freud's early comments on the subject through its present-day use as a therapeutic tool. In the introduction, the editors comment on the change from suppression of the analyst's feelings in a clinical situation to “genuine participation in an on-going process.” They attempt to demonstrate that countertransference is an ally of the therapeutic process rather than a hindrance as it was taken to be earlier. A stated aim is to lessen the polarization between interpersonal and intrapsychic schools. They are particularly interested in the use of countertransference as a key to resistance and in its integration into the formulation of treatment strategies, particularly the use of emotional communications with the patient.

The book is organized into three parts. Part I presents nine authors writing on “The Concept of Countertransference.” Issacharoff poses the question, “What process can give us the feeling that we know something about the patient and about ourselves?” His answer, of course, is countertransference.

Theodore Laquercia

Theodore Laquercia

Theodore Laquercia  

This book is a survey of the work of Sigmund Freud during the years 1886 to 1905, during which period the major formulations of his theory of neuroses were made. His major works, Studies on Hysteria (1895), The Interpretation of Dreams (1899), and Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905), provided the fundamentals of psychoanalysis, encompassing the major theoretical and technical thrust of his work which remained, though these were modified and amplified continually until his death in 1939.

In tracing the development of Freud's early theories, the author sets out to “show that Freud's interest in the neuroses was shaped by contemporary medical trends toward a greater concern with these diseases… closely tied to current medical and psychological literature [and that] Freud, from his first studies of the neuroses, consistently eschewed speculations concerning possible organic explanations and concentrated instead on the psychological interpretation of neurotic symptoms.”

Levin offers a well-documented presentation of the literature that was available to Freud and demonstrates many similarities between his work and that of others in the nineteenth century. The contention that he was especially influenced by the “Heimholtz School” (because of his work with Ernst Brücke and Theodor Meynert, well-known neurophysiologists of his day) is challenged. The author cites many other scholars whose work came to bear on Freud's thinking, notably the psychologist Johann Friedrich Herbart whose theories on psychic conflict formed a basis of Freud's early writings. The concept of unconscious mental phenomena is also widely discussed as is childhood sexuality.

What relationship exists between the academic background of psychoanalytic candidates and the psychoanalytic techniques they use at various levels of training?

This slim but comprehensive volume is the first in a Wiley series on Methods in Psychotherapy. Written by the dean of London

241

Jungians, the theorist who has done the most to extend Jung's theories to early childhood development and one of the editors of Jung's Collected Works, Fordham's study is a distillation of the mature thinking of a highly creative analyst. With his subtitle A Study in Analytical Psychology, Fordham wishes to establish that analytical psychology is “a discipline in its own right”, (p. ix), not restricted to the works of Jung that are at its base.

There are today at least three distinct Jungian treatment approaches. Dr. Fordham represents a branch of the London school of Jungians, a group which attempts in the treatment of patients to combine Jung's archetypal theory, especially his approach to dreams, with Fordham's own maturational schema; many of the forms of psychoanalysis, including couch use and up to five weekly treatment sessions, are used. This approach contrasts with that of the classical Jungian school, which is centered in Zurich, but is well represented in Germany, England, and America also. In the classical system the key element is the archetypal amplification of unconscious material. Its aim is to help the individual place his personal psychology and complexes within a wider historical frame of reference, and to transform his suffering by making a connection with the underlying collective substrate. It also contrasts with the perspective of James Hillman and his followers in archetypal psychology, for whom the empirical side of Jung is primary. The therapeutic task as seen by this group is to work as closely as possible with the exact images the psyche produces. The analyst is to guide the patient more deeply into the image so that he discovers the environment which is a suitable home for that image. Healing is presumed to come from the image's taking root in its own soil, like a plant that flourishes in just the right earth. In both these approaches, frequency of treatment hours is not the important variable; the material is the key.

As the number of women therapists increases, the study of the effects of the sex of the therapist on treatment becomes meaningful. Patients may choose, and mental health agencies may assign therapists of either gender, yet there are no guidelines for such pairing.

Meltzoff and Kornreich (1970), in reviewing the literature on sex-pairing in psychotherapy, conclude: “At present there is no clear basis for preferential assignment of a patient of either sex to a therapist of either sex. No statement can be made with confidence about the relative benefits of selected sex pairing with given types of patients.” More recently, a small, consistent body of literature has developed that permits some definitive statements about how patients differentially perceive, experience, and behave according to the therapist's gender.

It is clear from the literature that patients and analysts are susceptible to sex-linked stereotyped ideas that critically affect treatment decisions. Given freedom of choice, patients almost invariably choose men as therapists (Fuller, 1963; Chesler, 1971), and a recent survey shows that the clients of women therapists are primarily women (Pendergrass, 1974). Two explanations are possible: patients are disproportionately attracted to male therapists, or they actively avoid female therapists. Reasons patients give for seeking male therapists support both explanations: feeling greater respect for and confidence in a man's competence and authority, feeling more comfortable with and relating better to men, discomfort with women, fear and mistrust of women as authorities, embarrassment about discussing sexual matters with women (Chesler).

Muriel Sackler  

Thirty to fifty percent of the students registered in introductory biology in a community college where I teach can be expected to drop or fail the course. Most of them express the desire to learn. They expect high grades, but are unable to function in a way that will allow them to earn the grades they say they want. They are excessively absent and late, forget books and assignments, do not participate in classroom discussion. They talk or are otherwise occupied during lectures, act bored, tired or uninterested, or they sleep. Modification of content taught in the conventional way yields the same results.

Studies indicate that most learning difficulties are engendered by emotional conflicts within the learner which may arise in response to the teacher, the learning situation or the emotional significance of learning in the learner's personal life (Pearson, 1954; Love and Strean, 1963; Ekstein and Motto, 1969; Hill, 1971; Kirman, 1977). Difficulties also result from cultural deprivation, with consequent lack of impulse control and ability to learn (Lustman, 1970).

Reports (Kornrich, 1965) show that the majority of underachievers have the intelligence necessary to fulfill their educational requirements and that interference in intellectual learning results from emotional factors which render them unready to learn.

This book has the stated purpose of “elucidating and liberating the use of illness as figures of speech and lurid metaphors,” but the book actually turns into an irrational, strident attack against the concept of emotional factors in cancer.

The New York Times book review of July 16, 1978 observed, “It is a deeply personal book, pretending for the sake of decency to be a thesis.” Neither the reviewer nor the author divulged the nature of the personal problem. Put on its publication date, Susan Sontag gave a press interview in which she discussed her marriage and divorce problems, her devotion to her 17-year-old son and medical conquest of her cancer.

The first part of the book is a sprightly account of the historic attachment of metaphors to tuberculosis. Her allusions to the 19th century literary figures, including Shelley and Keats, who succumbed to TB make colorful, entertaining reading. But already in the introduction she exhibits an argumentative stance which makes this flawed work more irritating and disappointing than provocative, simplistic rather than thoughtful: “My point is that illness is not a metaphor, and that the most truthful way of regarding illness—and the healthiest way of being ill—is one most purified of, most resistant to, metaphoric thinking.”

This statement is implicitly anti-literary, surprisingly, as well as anti-psychoanalytic.

Introduction

In 1966 in a paper titled “Maturational Interpretations,” Dr. Spotnitz wrote, “The therapist does not intervene to reduce developmental needs directly … rather he intervenes to lay the foundation for new growth by freeing the patient from the stranglehold of pathological maladaptations” (p. 5).

The idea that interpretation of archaic defenses often falls on deaf cars and may even amplify a patient's opposition to treatment has also been described in great detail in the literature (Clevans, 1957; Kirman, 1976; Liegner, 1977; Love and Feldman, 1961; Love and Mayer, 1955; Meadow, 1974; Nelson, 1947; Ormont, 1964; Rosenthal, 1976). These analysts have described joining techniques and maturational approaches that have been effectively utilized in their analytic work with both individuals and groups.

More recently there has been much interest and discussion in modern analytic theory and treatment about the differentiation between the concepts of developmental needs, maturational interventions and maturational interpretations.

This paper defines and discusses the concept of maturational intervention, recounts the history and origin of the concept, and describes how it evolved at the Bronx office of the Jewish Board of Guardians from 1951 to 1953 in a study group for the diagnosis and treatment of borderline children and their parents.

Despite a title that suggests a discussion of methods of intervention other than interpretation, the focus of this book is on theory rather than on technique. Gedo believes that departures from classical technique are already accepted, and that they require corresponding changes in underlying theory.

247

Gedo narrowly defines interpretation as “statements that translate hitherto unconscious material into discursive language.” Thus it is a technical innovation, for example, to explore with a patient how he might arrange to pay for treatment because such a discussion is about overt behavior rather than unconscious material.

In another example, Gedo describes how he “responded only insofar as the analysand indicated… to control overstimulation… and to regulate tension.” Biological needs such as the need to return to tolerable levels of stimulation are, then, beyond interpretation because they are beyond the reach of subjectivity and introspection. Thus, the patient may require pacification (tension regulation), unification (integration of a coherent set of goals), or optimal disillusionment (reality testing). These practices, for patients who have not yet reached the oedipal level, are defended on the grounds that the therapeutic aim of psychoanalysis is the completion of interrupted developmental processes.

Modern analysts will not find their credulity taxed by the notion that there are patients who have never achieved the oedipal level—patients whose pathology does not represent a regression from some higher level of functioning. They will be familiar with such deviations from classical technique as exploration, confrontation, and the control of overstimulation by limiting interventions to the patient's attempts at contact.

The author's interest, however, is not in offering alternatives to interpretation, but in offering alternatives to classical theory. Gedo offers self-organization as a new paradigm for psychoanalytic psychology. He believes that mental life begins with uncoordinated goals from which a cohesive hierarchy of personal aims (the self-organization) is gradually integrated.

Introduction

Obesity is one of the most difficult problems to handle and successfully treat psychotherapeutically. The psychodynamics are extremely involved due to the oral fixation and the multiplicity of ctiological factors. The dynamics involved are characterized often by an insatiable need for love and at the same time defiant and spiteful behavior. Bruch (1973) points out that although modifications in psychotherapeutic approaches were changed significantly in respect to schizophrenia, borderline states and narcissistic personalities, the concepts in treating obesity, seen as “expressions of oral dependency, incorporative cannibalism, rejection of pregnancy … still follow the classical psychoanalytic model.”

This article will discuss the dynamics of a narcissistic character disturbance, the form of which has shown itself most conspicuously in severe overweight, dating from early childhood. The focus will be on the relationship between the resolution of specific narcissistic factors and weight loss.

Theoretically, obesity represents fixation or regression to the oral phase of development, where overeating seems to relate to the repressed oral aggressive drives of the patient.

Under the title of paradigmatic therapy, Marie Coleman Nelson (1968) has presented an interesting style of treatment for use with certain borderline patients, and she has developed a theoretical perspective for understanding its results. As is so often true of technical innovations, the method is not only useful in practice but helps to elucidate the nature of psychotherapy. In particular, paradigmatic therapy brings into relief the relationship between the roles of attitudes and information in the process of therapy.

Nelson (1962) has illustrated the paradigmatic approach with a transcribed hour, and provided it with a rationale which is further expanded in another essay (1967) where it is joined by a metapsychological theoretical construction. I shall assume that the reader is familiar with the transcribed hour since it cannot be summarized without introducing the theoretical perspectives to be discussed in this paper. I shall first discuss Nelson's rationale for her approach, indicating where I think the emphasis should fall. Then I will briefly state my understanding of what occurs during the sample hour.

The Significance of the Resolution of Group Resistance in Group Analysis

Leslie Rosenthal

Leslie Rosenthal

12 West 96th St.
New York, N.Y. 10025

Leslie Rosenthal  

Freud emphasized the profound significance of the resolution of resistance both for the patient and for the treatment. In his Introductory Lectures on Psychoanalysis he stated:

Analytic treatment makes as great demands for efforts on the part of the patient as on the physician, efforts to abolish the inner resistances. The patient's mental life is permanently changed by overcoming these resistances, is lifted to a higher level of development and remains proof against fresh possibilities of illness. The labor of overcoming the resistances is the essential achievement of the analytic treatment.

(Freud, 1916-17, p. 377)

Through the vehicle of resistance the psychoanalytic patient conveys the message that he is incapable of engaging consistently in spontaneous, emotionally significant verbal communication. In its early view psychoanalysis saw resistance as the withholding of information. It is now understood as an inadequate, maladaptive and indirect form of self-revelation.

In the group setting resistance is recognized as the voluntary and involuntary (conscious and unconscious) methods by which group members avoid giving spontaneous and emotionally significant verbal expression to their life histories, feelings and thoughts.

In the group these are multi-directional and may operate in relation to the therapist, one or more fellow members or the whole group.

The Concept of Countertransference as Therapeutic Instrument: Its Early History

Claire Ernsberger

Claire Ernsberger

220 West 71st Street
New York, N.Y. 10003

Claire Ernsberger  

In current psychoanalytic literature, scarcely a paper containing clinical material fails to take account of countertransference, at least in passing. That some countertransference is objective and may be a useful therapeutic tool is by now the prevailing view. Writings on countertransference by psychoanalysts of nearly all schools commonly refer to such well-known proponents of that view as Winnicott, Spotnitz, Racker, and Scarles. The modern school, which began with the work of Spotnitz, accepts the idea of objective countertransference as one of its bases and has studied and continues to study and develop a theory of technique that utilizes the objective countertransference responses not only as a way of understanding the patient but also as the source for interventions meant to resolve resistances.

This was not, of course, always the state of things. From 1910, when Freud coined the word (Gugeniibertragung) and admonished the therapist to “recognize this … in himself and overcome it,” until about the end of the 1960's, an evolution in psychoanalytic thinking occurred—from the early belief that countertransference was simply a hindrance to treatment, to the currently prevailing view. The valuable work that has been done since 1969—and there has been a great deal—has proceeded in an atmosphere of general willingness to consider these ideas and of general concurrence in at least the basic premises.

Children diagnosed as having a borderline syndrome present varying developmental problems. A body of published knowledge based on clinical experience has gradually emerged, emphasizing the crucial impact of the resolution of the early mother-child symbiosis on the growth of object relationships and ego strength nuclei (Eckstein and Wallerstein, 1957; Fintzy, 1971; Glovacchini, 1972; Mahler, 1968, 1971, 1975; Masterson, 1977).

Borderline children are characterized by variations in stability of behavioral control, in integration of thought and affect, and in potential for regression into schizophrenic psychosis. Their defenses remain developmentally primitive, and their lack of effectiveness in warding off anxiety contributes to symptom formation. The absence of an integrated sense of self; the splitting of self and object representations; poor frustration tolerance; emergence of primary process content; and temporary disintegration of thought processes and reality testing may all be noted in borderline children. Destructive or self-destructive acting out seems to be used as a means of reintegrating the self and lowering anxiety. Despite underlying ego deficits on a social level, at times these children can be quite appropriate. They also may appear merely neurotic and beset with phobias, somatic symptoms and overt anxiety.

In his most recent book, the historian and social critic Christopher Lasch has written a most interesting analysis of modern American society. The title of the book carries a double meaning, referring to our narcissistic culture as well as to the social medium in which it was cultivated. Reformulating the Role of Aggression

Harold Davis

Harold Davis

3 Rutherford Place
New York, N.Y. 10003

Harold Davis  

In 1940 Freud observed that: “All of psychoanalysis has to be reformulated in terms of understanding the aggressive drive as separate from the libidinal drive.” Now, forty years later, it is clear that this task has yet to be accomplished, for the psychoanalytic theory of aggression is still the poor relative of libidinal theory. Although there has been lately a growing clinical interest in aggression, most analysts have yet to pay as much attention to the aggressive feelings and behavior of their clients as they pay to their client's libidos.

The psychoanalytic theory of aggression had its origins in Freud's “Little Hans” paper of 1909, in which he argued that aggression is one of the self-preserving instincts, rejecting Adler's view that aggression is an instinct in its own right, independent of the sexual and self-preservative instincts. The matter rested there until ten years later when Freud formulated his famous death-instinct theory, in which he elevated the aggressive instinct to equal status with the libidinal instinct (redefined to include both sexual and life-preserving instincts). The aim of this new aggressive instinct was no longer to preserve life but to destroy it. And, just as the libidinal instinct proceeded from narcissistic self-love to object love, so the aggressive instinct, originally narcissistically self-destructive, was turned outward and proceeded from primary masochism to sadism.

Robert Welber

Robert Welber

Robert Welber  

Of the spectrum of developmental ages and stages from birth through death, many analysts have concluded that the most difficult stage to understand and analyze is adolescence. The induced feelings,

244

the fuzzy es between developmental tasks and unuseful, destructive defenses, as well as the impulsivity of this stage has made patients of this age difficult to diagnose and treat.

Peter Blos in his collected works, The Adolescent Passage: Developmental Issues, offers an enlightened and meaningful work on adolescence including his own innovative theories that are based on forty years of psychoanalytic practice with children, adolescents, and their families. He indicates that practitioners who work with children will understand and have an easier time with adolescents, for the roots of problems and resolutions of this stage are to be found in early childhood rather than in maladaptive adult behavior.

Blos' background is scientific. He came from the study of biology over forty years ago into the field of psychoanalysis and was influenced by August Aichhorn and Anna Freud; he has taken into account Margaret Mahler's theories as well as those of many others.

The book has nineteen papers arranged into six sections. The first five sections cover an overview of adolescents and their environment, normal stages of male and female adolescence, acting out and delinquency, psychic structure and body image. Each section has an introduction. The final section is a summary of the author's contributions to the psychoanalytic theory of adolescence.

Perhaps the most meaningful of his contributions is the idea of a second individuation process of adolescence, encompassing a reworking of the original pre-oedipal and oedipal stages. This process is a continuation of the earlier process. Blos states he does not see a resolution of the oedipal conflict in the early years, but rather a suspension of it through the latency years, and a revival at the onset of puberty. The adolescent needs to regress, not as a defense, but finally to work through the unfinished business of early childhood, where he began to separate emotionally, internalize, and identify.

Gerald Lucas

Gerald Lucas

Gerald Lucas  

The body of this book consists of six case histories provided by six different psychoanalysts supervised by Heinz Kohut. Each of the cases had begun before Kohut had formulated his psychology of the self. In the first three cases the therapist was under the impression that the patient's correct diagnosis was a psychoneurosis or neurotic character disorder. This diagnosis was taken to mean that the core problem of the patient was a conflict between the psychic structures of id, ego and superego concerning oedipal or incestuous strivings and that a classical transference to the analyst would develop. Since such a transference did not develop, each of these cases had to be rediagnosed as narcissistic personality disorders as defined by Kohut (1971, 1977). The patients' complaints are consistent with this diagnosis: unable to perform adequately, dissasatisfied with the job, lack of direction and initiative, preoccupied with unhappiness, depression or depression masked by compulsive promiscuity or voyeurism, need for external stimulation to become perked up, lack of enjoyment in sex, and a sense of missing cohesiveness and inner firmness. The transferences took the forms elucidated by Kohut: mirror transferences and idealizing transferences. In mirror transferences the grandiose (omnipotent) self of the infane is remobilized and the analyst is treated as either an extension of the grandiose self, or as someone similar to it (twinship or alter ego transference), or as a person with special relationship to the self (mirror transference in the narrow sense). In idealizing transferences the analyst is attributed all the idealizations which the infant had transferred from himself onto the parent when his narcissism had been shattered.

The discrepancy between the original and final diagnosis is significant for one of the goals of this book. The Psychology of the Self is concerned with demonstrating the superiority of Kohut's new psychology. The analysts who had been trained in classical psychoanalytic diagnosis and treatment missed important clues and misinterpreted the patients' communications in a treatment destructive way until the new views took hold.

Claire Ernsberger  

Harold Searles has been studying, treating, and writing about schizophrenia and psychotic disorders for the past thirty years. The

252

treatment of such disorders, it is now widely recognized, requires the study and understanding of the phenomenon of countertransference, and Searles has been a frequent contributor to the psychoanalytic literature on this subject. This book, however, is not, strictly speaking, a major work on the subject of countertransference. It is a collection of Searles' papers on all subjects written since the publication of his previous collection, Schizophrenia and Related Subjects, in 1965. Countertransference is, of course, a subject of continuing interest to the author; some of the chapters here are devoted to it exclusively, and some barely touch on it in passing. Most are concerned with it in some way because of Searles' general focus on treating patients who arouse strong countertransferential feelings.

All the chapters in this volume have appeared previously as journal articles or chapters in anthologies. The value of the book is that it provides the reader with one source within which all of this interesting writer's work of the last fourteen years may be found. The papers are presented in chronological order of first presentation (either as an address or as a written article), so the reader is afforded the opportunity to follow the development of Searles' thought on various analytic subjects over this period of time. In recent years Searles has devoted most of his time to private practice (along with lecturing and teaching) and has, therefore, worked with a wider variety of patients than he saw during his years at Chestnut Lodge. He has discovered, then, that the analysis and use of countertransference is essential when working with patients who “vary widely in the kinds and degrees of emotional illness from which they suffer”—not only the psychoses, but the less severe disorders as well.

The Concept

Freud (1905) regarded transference as one of the two pillars of psychoanalysis, the other being resistance. In his metaphor, transferences are “new editions or facsimiles” of old emotional experiences, and “they replace some earlier person by the person of the physician.” In a similar vein, Greenson (1967) defines transference as “the experience of feelings to a person which do not befit that person and which actually apply to another. Essentially, a person in the present is reacted to as though he were a person in the past.” Until recent times in clinical theory, “the past” was understood to refer to the patient's oedipal period and the “earlier person” to a significant object of that period whose characteristics the patient now attributes to the analyst.

The ego of the oedipal child is relatively advanced in terms of function and identity. Self and object, child and parent, are perceived by the child as separate entities. When this situation is later replicated in the transference, the patient who is fixated at the oedipal period sees the analyst as a clearly delineated object who represents an earlier well-defined parental figure, both differentiated from the patient's self, past and present.

The Shared Experience: A Theory of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy

Martin Fisher

Martin Fisher

360 E 65th Street
New York, N.Y., 10021

Martin Fisher  

The definitions, clarifications and descriptions of the process of psychoanalytic psychotherapy continue to be unclear and elusive. I believe that the problem lies, not in discovering unitary and agreed upon conceptualizations, but in accepting the notion of coexisting definitions and descriptions. An impasse has been created in the growing field of theories and psychodynamic therapy by the tendency of theorists (Freud, Jung, Adler, Rank, Sullivan, etc.) to imply or insist that one system or explanation of personality theory and/or therapy is the “word,” excluding other conceptualizations and formulations. On one issue however most theorists would agree: Freud's greatest discovery was that heretofore seemingly unexplainable behavior (i.e., conversion symptoms, compulsions, obsessive thoughts, etc.) was anything but capricious. These behaviors have come to be seen as symptomatic of explainable and predictable psychic and/or real events based upon the new and exciting discoveries of psychoanalysis. Subsequent developments from 1895 until the present are now history, and the evolution of our search, research and philosophical growth continues.

The impetus for the thoughts and conceptual notions in what follows has grown out of this writer's work with patients in modern psychoanalytic therapy. Much more important, however, was my own return to psychoanalysis during my middle years.

Introduction

When the patient came to consult me and ask for psychoanalytic assistance, she was twenty-five years of age and already at an advanced stage of her illness. In view of the malignant nature of the metastasizing melanoma, any hope of recovery was unfounded. The therapeutic relationship developed into the psychoanalysis of a personality which had been severely disturbed in infancy, whereby the patient was now suffering from an organically spreading disease. Concerning the therapeutic result of the 300 therapy sessions over a period of two years, it is the writer's belief that the patient's life was prolonged and her physical suffering was considerably diminished. By way of illustration, the patient hardly needed to take analgesics at all

This more or less objective result is, however, not as important as the subjective psychic benefits which the patient seemed to have gained from the therapy. We succeeded in elaborating a relatively coherent picture of the psychogenesis of the cancer. Although the following sections deal primarily with the difficulties that the patient and therapist had with each other, this should not obscure the fact that the patient went through a genuine process of self-recognition.

Current Variations in Theory and Practice

The editors have chosen five articles submitted to Modern Psychoanalysis describing case treatments based on variant theoretical approaches. Evelyn Liegner's article, Solving a Problem of Counter-transference Resistance in a Case of Psychosis, describes several joining and reflecting techniques used by this modern psychoanalyst to resolve a difficult resistance. Lawrence Friedman's paper, Marie Coleman Nelson's Paradigmatic Therapy: A Variant Reading, critiques a transcribed therapy hour of Marie Coleman Nelson and gives his views on the consequences in the patient-analyst relationship of this analyst's style of communicating.

Coexisting definitions and descriptions of events in psychotherapy have led to an impasse, according to Martin Fisher. In The Shared Experience: A Theory of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, Fisher discusses the concepts of trust and mutuality and their use in therapy from the existentialist's point of view.

In Melanoma: Its Relationship to Inner Emptiness in a Psychoanalytic Case Study, Martin Kahleyss attempts to uncover the roots of a cancer patient's organic illness in emotional disturbances of infancy. The significance of feelings of emptiness to her illness is connected with the inability to picture the missing part object. Kahleyss summarizes his exploration of the symbolic representations produced by his patient during 275 sessions.

In James B. McCarthy's article, Infantile Narcissism: a Study of Symbiosis and Aggression in Borderline Children, his perceptive study of the canine hero in Jack London's Call of the Wild details the analysis of the narcissistic interaction between dog and master as it parallels this kind of interaction in humans.

Background

Through modern psychoanalysis, an acting out, psychotic schizophrenic patient can be enabled to become a cooperative and well-functioning analytic patient. Contrary to the commonly held view, such a patient is capable of transference attachments, albeit narcissistic transference rather than object (oedipal) transference. I suggest that psychosis, regardless of culture and etiology, may have a specific meaning; that its symptoms, ideas of reference, hallucinations and paranoid ideation serve the specific defensive purpose of warding off life-threatening impulses (suicidal and homicidal); and that psychotic schizophrenia is a psychologically reversible disease when treated by modern psychoanalysis.

The treatment of a single patient will be reported, with detailed recording and analysis of the processes occurring within the patient; the induced feelings (objective and subjective countertransference) of the analyst; and the transformation of these feelings by the analyst into therapeutic communications within the dyadic relationship.
